The early life history of Amblema plicata begins with a brief period of endotrophic development following syngamy. Laboratory observations indicate that at a water temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], the interval from ovum activation to hatching lasts approximately 10 days [ab = approximately 10 days]. Upon eclosion, the newly emerged glochidium possesses a minute shell measuring roughly 0.02 cm [Lb = roughly 0.02 cm] across the prodissoconch. This initial size is consistent with the small-born offspring typical of freshwater unionid mussels that rely on a parasitic larval stage. Shortly thereafter, at the point of larval settlement onto a suitable fish host, the shell length increases to approximately 0.03 cm . This settlement-stage dimension represents the size at which the glochidium attaches to host gill or fin tissue and begins its brief obligate parasitic phase. The duration of this encapsulated period is tightly regulated by temperature, and growth during this post-hatching interval remains limited, as the larva depends entirely on yolk reserves until it completes metamorphosis and detaches as a free-living juvenile.

Following metamorphosis and excystment from the fish host, the juvenile bivalve enters a prolonged phase of benthic growth in the riverine substrate. Field surveys of Amblema plicata populations in the Mississippi River basin have documented that puberty, marked by the onset of gametogenesis, is attained at a shell length of 5 cm [Lp = 5 cm]. This size at sexual maturation is a critical life-history threshold, as individuals below this length do not engage in reproductive activity. The age at which this size is achieved varies with local stream productivity and thermal regime, but the 5 cm benchmark provides a consistent metric for identifying the transition to the reproductively active portion of the population. Individuals that surpass this length begin to allocate resources toward gonad development rather than exclusively toward somatic growth. Puberty therefore represents a fundamental shift in the energy budget of the mussel, with consequences for population dynamics and recruitment success across its range.

Reproductive output in reproductively mature females of Amblema plicata has been quantified through direct counts of glochidia released during spawning events. At a stable water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], a female with a shell length of 7.85 cm releases approximately 325,709 glochidia over the annual spawning season [Ri = approximately 325,709 glochidia over the annual spawning season] during a single extended reproductive period each year [F_R_i = tended reproductive period each year]. This daily fecundity rate, based on seasonal brooding observations, reflects the continuous release of glochidia over the reproductive period rather than a single discrete spawning event. The high fecundity compensates for the extremely low survival probability of individual larvae, characteristic of unionid mussels where parasitic larval attachment success depends on encountering a suitable and immunologically compatible fish host, a stochastic event in large river systems.

The maximum shell length attained by Amblema plicata under natural conditions has been determined from extensive museum collections and long-term mark-recapture studies. The ultimate shell length recorded for this species is 11.5 cm [Li = 11.5 cm], a value that represents the asymptotic size approached by the oldest individuals in stable habitats. Corresponding to this maximal linear dimension, the estimated ultimate wet weight, derived from length-weight regressions corrected for tissue density, is 54.7 grams [Wwi = 54.7 grams]. This body mass reflects the substantial accumulation of shell material and somatic tissue over a long lifespan. The relationship between length and wet weight in this species follows a cubic function consistent with general bivalve allometry, and the 54.7 gram value serves as a useful benchmark for assessing individual condition and comparing growth performance across different river reaches or impoundment regimes.

Longevity is a prominent feature of the life cycle of Amblema plicata, with individuals capable of persisting for many decades under favorable conditions. In populations inhabiting stable, silt-free substrates with consistent flow regimes, the maximum recorded lifespan reaches approximately 53 years [am = approximately 53 years] at a water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. This extraordinary duration places Amblema plicata among the longer-lived members of its family, Unionidae. The attainment of such an advanced age is facilitated by a low metabolic rate and a robust shell that provides effective protection against predation and physical disturbance. This extended lifespan also has significant demographic consequences, as it allows for multiple reproductive events across many years, effectively buffering the population against occasional years of poor recruitment. Natural mortality in this species is typically attributed to senescence-related physiological decline rather than to predation.
